key_insight: The Personal Imitation Game asks a tougher question than whether AI sounds human: can it convincingly imitate a specific person? A study with 30 participants establishes a human baseline and identifies writing style, personality, and biographical facts as key identity signals.
problem_solved: Traditional imitation tests assess generic human-like conversation, not whether an AI can reproduce the distinctive identity of a particular individual.
method: Introduce a conversational evaluation framework focused on imitating a specific individual.
Test with 30 participants to establish a human baseline and examine the identity cues interrogators use.
Propose an LLM-based system to demonstrate the framework; implementation details and results are not available in the provided, truncated abstract.
impact: The framework gives AI/ML practitioners a way to evaluate person-specific imitation beyond general conversational fluency. It also highlights identity cues relevant to personalized assistants and impersonation-risk assessment.
visual_elements: Side-by-side comparison: classic Turing Test—'Is it human?' versus Personal Imitation Game—'Is it this person?'
Conversation diagram linking an interrogator, a target individual, and an AI imitator.
Three identity-signal icons: writing style, personality, and biographical facts.
A 30-person pictogram representing the human-baseline study.
paper_title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
paper_authors: Muhammad Rizky Wellyanto, Hajara-Yasmin Isa, Kexin Xue, Vishal Ravichandran, Wenpeng Lu
